28. He submitted that in view of the provisions of section 171 the Special Judge is obliged to follow the procedure laid down under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 to try the offences under Chapter XXI as, if such offences were offences specified in the Schedule thereto but learned Special Judge, 5th Court was most illegally following the procedure laid down by the EP Rules, which made the trial vitiated. 

 30. In support of his submissions, he cited [Hagi Ali Mohammad vs CIT: [1940] 08ITR 243; Rajmani Devi vs CIT: [J937] 5 ITR 631; Mohammad Hayat vs CIT: [1937] 5 ITR 159; Dhuni Chand Dhani Ram vs CIT: AIR 1926 Lahore 161; Nirmal Kumar Singh vs Secretary of State: 2 ITC 20; Kesaridas and Sons vs CIT: 2 ITC 213; Ram Pratap Sukh Dial vs CIT: 3 ITC 362; Harmukhrai Dulchand vs CIT: 3 ITC 198; Messrs Burn &Co. [J934] 2 ITR 30; Jawala Prasad Chobey vs CIT: [1935] 3 LTR 295; Maharaja Patiala vs CIT: [1943] 11 ITR 202; V Srinivas Naichen vs Agricultural Income-tax Officer: [1963] 47 ITR 122; P V Pai vs R L Rinawma, DCI: [1993] 200 ITR rt n ITO vs S K H abibullah: [1962] 44 ITR 809 SC; CIT vs Khemchand and Ramdas: [l938] 6 ITR 414 PC; American Express Bank vs Chairman, NBR: 54 DLR 06; P Jayappan vs S K Perumal: [1984] 149 ITR 697 SC; CIT vs Chowdhury Ramzan Ali and another: 34 DLR 278 AD; Dr. MO Ghani vs A N M Mahmood: 18 DLR 463 SC; Nagina Silk Mill vs ITO: 15 DLR 18 SC; Anisminic Ltd. vs Foreign Compensation Commission: [1969] 2 AC 147 HL at 195; MD Rupali Bank Ltd Tafazal Hossain: 44 DLR (AD) 260; Nazrul Islam Chowdhury vs State: 1999 BLD 18 AD; Nesar Ahmed vs Government of Bangladesh: 49 DLR (AD) 111 Suraj Mall Mobta and Co. vs AV Visvanatha Sastri and another: [1954] 26 1TR 01 SC] and Dhakeswari Cotton Mills Ltd vs CIT: [1954] 26 ITR 775 SC, which shall be considered at the time of consideration of the relevant issue. 

 Chapter XXI comprising sections 164 to 171, which is very relevant for our purpose creating certain obligations, false statement in the verification of the income tax returns, concealment of income, etc as punishable offences. Section 169 provides for sanction for prosecution. Section 170 empowers the Commissioner to compound any offence punishable under the Ordinance either before or after the institution of the proceeding or prosecution for an offence. Section 171 empowers a Special Judge appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958 to punish any offence under this chapter as if such offence were specified in the schedule to that Act. Chapter XXII comprises sections 172 to 184D providing for miscellaneous matters for correction of errors, computation of limitation, service of notice, bar of suits and prosecution, etc. Section 184 regarding restriction on registration of documents was omitted by Finance Act, 1992. Chapter XXIII comprising sections 185 to 187 empowers, inter alia, the Board to make rules and provides for repeal and savings. Section 187 empowers the government by notification in the official gazette to make such provisions as it think fit for removing any difficulty that may arise in giving effect to any of the provisions of the Ordinance. However, no notification shall be issued under this section after the thirtieth day of June, 1988. 

 44. Reading the entire Ordinance, it appears that the Ordinance was promulgated for replacing Income-tax Act, 1922 to update and consolidate the income tax law to raise revenue in the name of income tax for the Government. The income tax is a tax imposed on income. Income tax is popularly known as direct tax and forms major part of all other direct taxes and also substantial part of the revenue in the developed economies. If the entire provisions of the Ordinance are closely read, only objective to be achieved is assessment of the Income chargeable to tax and determination of the tax payable thereon. Penal provisions that are provided are intended to enforce payment of tax and discourage evasion thereof with the pain of going to the jail, which would be considered little later. 

 (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), or in any other law for the time being in force, an offence punishable under 'this Chapter, other than an offence under section 168, shall be tried by a Special Judge appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 (XL of 1958), as if such offence were an offence specified in the Schedule to that Act. 

 "It is clear that if persons dealt with by the impugned Act are deprived of substantial and valuable privileges, which they would otherwise have if they were dealt with under the Indian Income-tax Act, in that situation it is no defence to say that the discriminatory procedure also advances the course of justice. The matter has to be just from the point of view of the ordinary reasonable man and not from the point of view of the government. The ordinary reasonable man would say, when the stakes are heavy and serious charges of evasion of income tax was made against him, why one person similarly placed should have the advantage substantially of the procedure prescribed by the Indian Income-tax Act, while another person similarly situated be deprived of it." 

 147. The issue raised was whether the provisions of Chapter XXC were bad in law as there was no provision for giving the concerned parties an opportunity of being heard before an order could be passed under the provisions of section 269UD of the said Chapter for purchase by the Central Government of an immovable property agreed to be sold in an agreement of sale. 

 157. Section 3 of the Ordinance enumerated the classes of income tax authorities with the National Board of Revenue at the top. For constitution of the Board and the matters connected therewith the President's Order No. 76 of 1972 was made by the Notification dated 30-6-72, which came into force on 16-12-71. Clause (a) of article 2 of said Order defines the Board as the National Board of Revenue constituted under the provision of the Order and the Government as the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 (i) as soon as may be after commencement of this Order the government shall constitute a Board to be called the National Board of Revenue. 

 (ii) The Board shall consist of such number of members as may be appointed by the Government. 

 (iii) The Government shall appoint one of the members of the Board to be its Chairman. 

 (iv) The Board shall subject to the control of the government exercise such powers and perform such duties as may be entrusted to him by the Government or by or under any law. 

 (v) Without prejudice to the provision of clause (4), the Board shall exercise all the powers and perform all the duties, which immediately before the commencement of this Order, were being performed by the Central Board of Revenue constituted under the Central Board of the Revenue Act, 1924 (Act IV of 1924); by any government or under any law. 

 159. Article 3 clearly empowers the Government to constitute a Board to be called the National Board of Revenue comprising such number of members as may be appointed by the government. The Government shall then appoint one of the members as the Chairman of the Board. So, the Chairman must first be appointed a member of the Board. No one could be conceived of being appointed chairman who is not a member of the Board. His existence outside the Board cannot be conceived of under such Order. If the Board is not so constituted in accordance with the provisions of article 3 of the Order only legal consequence that would follow is that any power exercised and any duty performed by such Board would be vitiated for being coram non judice. 

 162. Article 4 of said Order also empowers the Government to make rules for the purpose of regulating the transaction of business by the Board and every order made or act done in accordance with such rules shall be deemed to be the order or act, as the case may, of the Board. Under clause (ii) any rules under clause (i) could be made so as to be retrospective from any date not earlier than the commencement of the Order and such rules may validate any acts done or order made by, or any proceedings of the Board or its Chairman or any of its members or Officers before making of such rules which, if done, made or taken after the commencement of the rules would not be inconsistent therewith. Clause (iii) further says no act, order or proceedings validated under clause (ii) shall be called in question merely on the ground that such act, order or proceeding was not valid at the time when it was done, made and taken. 

 163. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, on behalf of the Board, frankly said that no rules could have yet been made by the Government for the transaction of business by the Board under the Order. He wanted us to understand the transaction of business by the Board was being carried on under the rules and regulations that were made under the repealed Central Board of Revenue Act, 1924. Even after much labour and search, Mr Khan Saifur Rahman could not produce any regulations or rules for us. 

 165. In its wisdom the matters of revenue were vested not in one person but ina collective body of members of the Board. They were naturally expected to be expert in the field. How the Board could be run by a Chairman appointed from outside who was not even a member of the Board for so long could not be explained on behalf of the Board. How the Government could have left the matters of revenue in the hands of a secretary could not also be understood. 

 176. In the background of said context, he submitted that the present case along with a significant number of other cases, against those responsible for major corruption at the highest level of Government is the outcome of a coordinated effort pursuant to the national policy adopted in response to a national consensus. The Board is one of the key agencies engaged in the coordinated efforts to take effective action. The Board cooperated with the Anti-Corruption Commission and Bangladesh Bank and indeed, other relevant agencies of the Government. 

 180. It is true that evasion of tax generates black money and black money encourages corruption at the highest echelon of the Government and violence in the society. But we are unable to accept that the evasion of tax is the prime source of corruption in the economy. Could there be any economy found in the world which does not generate black money through evasion of tax either deliberately or unintentionally. The challenge every nation is facing against the black money is how to best and fast channelise the black money into the economy. That is why amnesty is declared in every advanced economy at a certain period of time to formalise or whiten such black money by payment of the tax on such undisclosed income at a rate that may be encouraging and enticing. 

 181. To prevent corruption the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 was promulgated and the Anti-Corruption Commission was recently reconstituted. All .these steps were taken in the right directions. But the revenue department should not be dragged into the works what are meant and specified for the Anti-Corruption Commission. The Ordinance was never designed to achieve such objective. In the course of carrying out the objective of the Ordinance which is designed to raise revenue for the Government, if the undisclosed incomes are disclosed and tax are realised there from that may only help reduce the black money in the circulation, that is all. 

 183. In order to succeed in the campaign against corruption, we must first find out the factors contributing to corruption or failing in the prevention of corruption. In various international researches, conditions found favourable to corruption are lacking control over accountability of the government, over-size of the government and/or excessive presence of governance in the life of the citizens, absence of access to the information of the decision making process at the high level of the government, absence of democracy or dysfunctional democracy, lacking civil society and non-governmental organisations which could monitor the government, weak rule of law, weak legal profession, weak judicial independence and lacking protection of the whistle blowers etc. are found to be the main contributors to corruption. 

 191. Mr Mahmudul Islam submitted on the impact of the proclamation dated 1-11-07 under Article 141B and 141C of the Constitution. He submitted that a proclamation under Article 141C does not have the effect of suspending the fundamental rights mentioned in the proclamation, but enforcement of those rights by the court shall remain suspended. It, does not mean that the Government can act contrary to those rights, but even if the Government so actsit cannot be assailed in Court as it would amount to enforcement of the fundamental fights which have been suspended. Read properly it means on the present case, power of this Division under Article 102(1) for enforcement of fundamental rights remains suspended. 

 192. He however, submitted that the proclamation dated 11-1-07 does not take way the powers of this Division under Article 102(2) and this Division can interfere if any Governmental action does not have any legal pedigree or, in other words, the Court can declare any action to be without lawful authority if it is not in conformity with the relevant law. 

 196. He submitted that exclusion of the income tax authority from the initiation of any proceeding under the Ordinance was not without any reason. During the drive against corruption under the state of emergency, the income tax authority could not be taken into confidence. He also complained, because of such rule the Special Judge most illegally was following the procedure laid down under the EP Rules along with the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958 and such procedure ought to be unlawful and without jurisdiction. 

 200. Section 3 of the EP Ordinance empowers the Government, by gazette notification, to make rules for maintaining the security and interest of the state and people or the economic life or prevention and prosecution of the corruption in various spheres of national life or ensuring the supply of essential goods and services, etc. By the Emergency Powers (Amendment) Ordinance, 2007 (Ordinance No.6 of 2007) following section 3(Ka) was inserted in the said Ordinance. 

 201. In view of such provisions; Mr Rafiqul Hug submitted that the Government was only empowered by the EP Ordinance amongst others, to investigate, prosecute or try one for any offence committed during the currency of the emergency. The submission that does not invite any two opinions thereon is however, not relevant in the case before us and can be decided in a properly constituted case, if need be. But it must be stated that the special judge exercising jurisdiction under section 171 of the Ordinance in the trial of the offences under Chapter XXI is obliged to follow the procedure laid down by the Code of Criminal Procedure as are consistent with the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. He would have no jurisdiction to try such offence in any procedure laid down by the EP Ordinance, 2007 or EP Rules, 2007. 

 204. Mr Mahmudul Islam was correct to submit that during the Emergency, when fundamental rights granted by Articles 36, 37, 38, 39, 40 and 42 remain suspended, the Government can make laws and take action in derogation of such rights. But a proclamation of emergency under Article 141 C does not have the effect of suspending the fundamental rights mentioned in the proclamation. Only enforcement of such rights shall remain suspended. Such proclamation cannot empower the Government to act contrary to those rights. But if the Government does so act, those actions cannot be assailed in any Court as that would amount to enforce said fundamental right, enforcement of which has been suspended. More precisely, enforcement of any fundamental right granted under Part-III shall remain suspended during the proclamation of emergency. Does he intend to say that such suspension would mean, any authority or tribunal could take any action or deal with the right, liberty, body, life, reputation or property of any citizen the way they think best, and such suspension would mean a licence for such an authority or tribunal to deal with the life, liberty, body and or property of the citizen. 

 209. It would be difficult to find out a nation that never faced a state of emergency in its history. The need to declare a state of emergency may arise from situations as diverse as an armed action against the state by internal or external elements, a natural disaster, civil unrest, an epidemic, a financial or economic crisis or a general strike. The implementation of emergency law invariably leads to restrictions on normal economic, civil or political activity and rights in order to address the extra-ordinary circumstances that have given rise to the emergency situation. Certain restrictions may be fully justified. At the same time, there is a danger at a government will take advantage of a state of emergency to introduce unwarranted restrictions on human rights and civil liberties, to neutralise political opponents, to postpone elections, or for other self-serving purposes that would be more difficult to pursue under normal circumstances. It is also in the experience, in some country there has been tendency to maintain state of emergency for years or even decade long after the original reason for its proclamation has disappeared. 

 212. The District Court dismissed the petition. The Court of Appeal affirmed the lower Court's decision on the view that there was no US Court that had jurisdiction over Guantanamo Bay. Then, the case reached the US Supreme Court. The sole question before the Supreme Court was, whether the foreign nationals in Guantanamo Bay might invoke the habeas corpus jurisdiction at all. Either US citizenship or Court jurisdiction was necessary for this invocation, and since the detainees were not citizens, US Court jurisdiction over Guantanamo Bay was at issue. According to the US treaty with Cuba over Guantanamo Bay, the US has "complete jurisdiction" over the base, but Cuba has "ultimate sovereignty." The government alleges that the fact that the treaty says this implies that the Courts have no jurisdiction; the detainees argue that regardless of what the treaty says, the US has full legal control in the area and should have jurisdiction. 

 214. Same date, the Supreme Court of USA also decided the case of Hamdi vs Rumsfeld. After the Congress passed a resolution-the Authorisation for Use of Military Force (AUMF)-empowering the President to "use all necessary and appropriate force" against "nations, organisations, or persons" that he determines "planned, authorised, committed, or aided" in the September 11, 2001, al Qaeda terrorist attacks, the President ordered the Armed Forces to Afghanistan to subdue al Qaeda and quell the supporting Taliban regime. Petitioner Hamdi, an American citizen whom the Government has classified as an "enemy combatant" for allegedly taking up arms with the Taliban during the conflict, was captured in Afghanistan and presently was detained at a naval brig in Charleston, SC. 

 215. Hamdi's father filed a habeas petition on his behalf under 28 USC 2241, alleging, among other things that the Government held his son in violation of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. Although the petition did not elaborate on the factual circumstances of Hamdi's capture and detention, his father asserted in other documents in the record that Hamdi went to Afghanistan to do "relief work" less than two months before September 11 and could not have received military training. 

 216. The Government attached to its response to the petition a declaration from Michael Mobbs (Mobbs Declaration), a Defence Department official. The Mobbs Declaration alleged various details regarding Hamdi's trip to Afghanistan, his affiliation there with a Taliban unit during a time when the Taliban was battling US allies, and his subsequent surrender of an assault rifle. 

 217. The District Court found that the Mobbs Declaration, standing alone, did not support Hamdi's detention and ordered the Government to turn over numerous materials for in-camera review. The Fourth Circuit reversed, stressing that, because it was undisputed that Hamdi was captured in an active combat zone, no factual inquiry or evidentiary hearing allowing Hamdi to be heard or to rebut the Government's assertions was necessary or proper, Concluding that the factual averments in the Mobbs Declaration, if accurate, provided a sufficient basis upon, which to conclude that the President had constitutionally detained Hamdi, the Court ordered the habeas petition dismissed. 

 223. The District Court granted habeas relief and stayed the commission proceedings, concluding that the President's authority to establish military commissions extends only to offenders or offences triable by such a commission under the law of war; that such law includes the Third Geneva Convention; that Hamdan is entitled to that Convention's full protections until adjudged, under it, not to be a prisoner of war; and that, whether or not Hamdan is properly classified a prisoner of war, the commission convened to try him was established in violation of both the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ), 10 U.S.C. $801 et seq., and Common Article 3 of the Third Geneva Convention because it had the power to convict based on evidence the accused would never see or hear. The DC Circuit reversed. Although it declined the Government's invitation to abstain from considering Hamdan's challenge, of: Schlesinger vs Councilman, 420 US 738, the appeals Court ruled, on the merits, that Hamdan was not entitled to relief because the Geneva Conventions are not judicially enforceable. The Court also concluded that Ex parte Quirin, 317 US I, foreclosed any separation-of- powers objection to the military commission's jurisdiction, and that Hamdan's trial before the commission would violate neither the UCMJ nor Armed Forces regulations implementing the Geneva Conventions. 

 231. In Haryana vs Bhajan Lal: (1992) SUPP(1) SCC 335, a case of political corruption against Bhajan Lal who was a Minister in 1977 when Devi Lal was the Chief Minister of Haryana. Bhajan Lal was the Chief Minister from 1982 to 1987. At the time of initiation of the criminal proceeding against corruption he was State Minister of Environment and Forest, Government of India. On the complaint of a political rival, Dharampal a case was registered under sections 161 and 165 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 on November 21 of 1987. Bhajanlal challenged the investigation on the basis of such FIR by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India which is similar to our Article 102.
